_README: The app's own tune, applied to the GR86 and read off nine screenshots on
2026-08-12. Same car, same parts as the default-tune fixtures, so this and
balance-gr86-default-2026-08-12.json are the C1 control pair: two whole
tunes on one build with nothing else moved.
READ c1_theDefaultTuneWins FIRST. It is the finding TESTS.md says outranks
every ordering in the discipline group, and it landed on the first car.

appTuneAsApplied._note: What is on the car. Where the app asked for something the game would not take exactly, the landed value is here and the asked-for value is in appAskedFor.

panel._note: Final state, after every tab was applied. The four earliest screenshots were taken mid-application and show 68.6/153.4, 8.817 and 138.2 — those are a partial tune and are not used.

c1_theDefaultTuneWins: THE GAME'S DEFAULT TUNE BEATS THE APP'S TUNE ON FIVE OF SIX PANEL COLUMNS,
on the same car, same parts, same sitting.
default      app        who wins
0-60                 3.317      3.333      default, by 1 frame
0-100                8.700      8.883      default, by 11 frames
top speed            141.1      137.4      default, by 3.7 mph
lateral G 60/120  1.25/1.41  1.26/1.42     app, by 0.01 at both speeds
TESTS.md C1: 'if the game's default tune beats the app outright in any
column, across more than one car, that column's formulas are wrong. That
outranks every ordering above.' This is one car, so the standing rule says
it is not yet general — but it is not one column either, it is five, and
the braking margin is not subtle.
THE BRAKING RESULT IS THE ONE TO CHASE. 5.2 ft longer from 60 mph is 8%,
and it is the app's own choices that could cause it: brake balance moved
50 -> 54% on the width-step rule that CLAUDE.md lists as a house heuristic
with no source at all, and the springs and damping are both far softer
than the game's. Case S4 sweeps balance and pressure against measured
stopping distance and is 15 minutes; it now has a specific thing to explain.
WHAT WOULD BE UNFAIR TO CONCLUDE. The app produced a road tune, and a road
tune trades braking and straight-line speed for cornering — which is
exactly what the lateral G column shows it buying, at both speeds. The
panel cannot see cornering except through that one number and cannot see
trail-braking stability at all. So this is not proof the tune is slower
round a lap. It IS proof that the app gives up a great deal on five
measurable columns to buy 0.01 g, and nothing in the app tells the user
that trade is being made.
NEXT: repeat on a second car before treating any column as settled, per the
standing rule. If braking loses on the second car too, the brake-bias rule
is the first thing to measure and the first thing to change.
axisPredictionFailed: PREDICTION MADE BEFORE THIS READING, in balance-ab-gr86-2026-08-12.json:
the axis tracks aero efficiency, so 0.743 should read about 157.
MEASURED: aero efficiency 0.743, AXIS 159.
The prediction is wrong and the aero hypothesis is dead in its simple form.
0.741 read 157 this morning and 0.743 reads 159 now; no smooth function of
aero efficiency jumps 2 mph across 0.002.
STATE OF THE AXIS QUESTION, with everything eliminated so far:
- final drive       ELIMINATED (held 157 across 3.50-4.60)
- top gear ratio    ELIMINATED (0.85 -> 0.75 -> 0.85, no change)
- aero efficiency   ELIMINATED (0.743 -> 159, 0.741 -> 157)
Only ONE reading of 157 has ever been taken on this car: the tune that was
already on it this morning, which was replaced before its settings were
captured. Everything since — default tune, 7th ratio moved, and now a
freshly generated app tune — reads 159. So the thing that produced 157 may
no longer exist anywhere, and the honest position is that the axis is 159
for every tune we can currently reproduce.
THE CANDIDATE NOT YET TESTED, and the obvious one on reflection: TIRE
PRESSURE. It is the standard lever on rolling radius, rolling radius sets
speed per rpm, and the axis is a speed scale. Both tunes measured at 159
sit at 31.0 and 31.5 psi. One reading settles it: change ONLY tire pressure
to something far away — 50 psi, or 20 — and read the axis.
IF PRESSURE DOES NOT MOVE IT EITHER, then nothing in the tune moves it, the
159 is a property of the build, and the single 157 was either a different
build state or a misread. At that point a stock GR86 becomes worth buying,
which is the condition written into MEASURE.md step 2.
aeroBalanceModelValidated: THE ADDITIVE MODEL SURVIVES A GENUINE TEST. It was fitted to two points
and had zero degrees of freedom left, so this third point is a real
prediction rather than a curve fit:
MEASURED                                          0.45   PASS
the dead simple model    202/457 = 0.4420  ->  prints 0.44   FAIL
So Aero Balance is front downforce plus a body term, over the total plus
both body terms, and the body terms are large — around 175 lb front and
215 lb rear on this car, comparable to the wings themselves. Case A1 called
this exactly.
STILL OWED: the rounding window makes the coefficients loose (the front
term is only pinned to somewhere between about 85 and 360 lb), and this is
all one car. A3's four floor-and-ceiling readings tighten the coefficients;
a second car tests whether the body terms are per-car, which they must be,
since they are the bodyshell.
NOTE THE APP GOT LUCKY HERE. It asked for aero as '60 % of range' front and
'71 % of range' rear, Boston eyeballed the slider positions, and the result
landed at AB 0.45 — inside the 0.42-0.48 target. That is a good outcome
from an instruction that cannot in principle target the readout, since a
percentage of two different pound ranges does not determine their ratio.
With the model solved the app can give the exact instruction instead.
mechBalanceNoModelFits: TWO WHOLE-TUNE ROWS NOW EXIST AND NO SIMPLE MODEL FITS BOTH.
bars F/R        bar ratio   springs F/R      spring ratio   MB
bars-only     predicts 0.68 and 0.51   ->  right once, wrong once
springs-only  predicts 0.50 and 0.56   ->  right once, wrong once
Each single-term model nails one row and misses the other, in opposite
directions. Solving the weighted model  MB = (arF + c.spF)/(sum)  for c
gives c = -2.36 on the default row and c = +0.0004 on the app row: not
merely different, opposite in sign. There is no c.
THE PREVIOUS COMMIT SAID 'a pure-spring ratio fits, MB is spring-led'. That
was one row and it is now dead too — the same one-point mistake as the aero
solve, made in the same hour.
WHAT THIS ACTUALLY ESTABLISHES, and it is worth having: WHOLE-TUNE
SNAPSHOTS CANNOT SOLVE MB. Every slider moved between these two rows, so
any model with two or more terms is underdetermined by construction, and
collecting more whole tunes will not help. This is the empirical
justification for MEASURE.md Phase 1's design — bars moved alone, springs
moved alone, one variable at a time — which until now was only an argument.
M1-M3 are five readings and they are now the highest-value five readings
available anywhere in the programme.
appDefects: FOUR THINGS THE APP GOT WRONG OR CANNOT EXPRESS, all found by applying it.
1. THE FIT IS READ ON THE WRONG GEARBOX. Boston: the fit is swept with the
DEFAULT gearing, because that is what is on the car before the app's tune
is applied. But the app then computes k = axis * fit * topRatio using
SPREAD's top ratio of 0.82, while the ratios in place when the fit was
read had a top gear of 0.85. The reading and the constant come from two
different gearboxes, and k is out by 0.82/0.85 = 3.5% as a direct result.
This is the SPREAD defect biting in the actual workflow, and it is the
clearest statement of it yet: EITHER the fit must be re-read after the
app's ratios are applied, OR the app must use the car's real top ratio.
2. SPRING RATES CANNOT BE HIT EXACTLY. Asked for 468 and 375, landed 468.1
and 374.9. Boston reports this is normal — always 0.1 to 0.2 off, rarely
exact. So the slider has its own grain, probably a fixed number of steps
across a car-specific range, and an integer lb/in target is not
reachable. Harmless to the tune, but the app implies a precision the
game does not offer, and the F/R RATIO is what the spring model rests on
— worth knowing the ratio lands slightly off what was computed.
3. AERO IS EMITTED AS A PERCENTAGE OF RANGE and the game takes pounds. See
aeroBalanceModelValidated: with the model solved this becomes an exact
instruction instead of an eyeballed one.
4. THE DEFAULT TUNE BEATS IT ON FIVE OF SIX COLUMNS. See c1.
casterRequest: Boston, unprompted: online sources say setting caster to 7 works and beats
what the in-game description implies, and he wants a caster test during the
fine-tuning phase. Recorded as a case rather than acted on.
Three caster values are now on the table for this car: the game's default
5.0, the app's road value 6.5 (from ForzaTune's 5.5-6.5 band, sitting at
the top of it), and the community's 7. The app is already at neither end
of the argument. Added to TESTS.md as case S7.
notes: The first four screenshots of this batch were taken while the tune was still being applied tab by tab: they show the app's tires, gearing, alignment and ARBs already set but the springs still at default, and the panel reads 68.6/153.4, 8.817 and 138.2. Those are a partial tune and are excluded from `panel`. Worth recording anyway as an accidental single-variable observation: applying the app's springs and ride height alone moved 0-100 from 8.817 to 8.883 and top speed from 138.2 to 137.4.
